# Per-site unsupervised ICS baselines and calibration for Modbus/BACnet on ProtoSense

## Verified facts
- ArmaturaSec states it has no confirmed attack capture from clients and only normal-traffic archives collected over three years. [F1]
- The company’s ProtoSense product is specified as passive protocol inspection for Modbus TCP and BACnet/IP traffic. [F2]
- A previous supervised classifier, fed public ICS data, produced so many false positives in real deployments that clients disabled alerts. [F3]
- The company requires on-device anomaly detection without affecting packet forwarding latency. [F4]
- The company requires alerts that can be explained to a plant manager in plain language. [F5]
- ArmaturaSec can dedicate one to two engineers part-time and give access to traffic archives, hardware bench, and firmware codebase under NDA. [F6]
- Kiss is open to joint projects with companies deploying ICS monitoring solutions and to contract research on anomaly-detection deployment. [F7]
- Kiss’s published work includes per-register Modbus/TCP baselines, a one-class Mahalanobis detector, and post-hoc threshold calibration using unlabelled operational data. [F8]

## Our inference
- Kiss’s documented testbed lists Modbus/TCP and DNP3 generators, not BACnet/IP; this suggests BACnet samples for the first experiment must come from ArmaturaSec archives or a new generator, and transfer remains to be tested.
- Her per-register baselines and post-hoc calibration are likely relevant to no-label, per-site detection, but the prior alert-fatigue failure means false-alarm acceptance, not detection accuracy alone, is the main operational risk.
- Kiss’s availability is unknown in the material, so the joint-project timeline is conditional; her openness to the format is not a confirmed commitment.

## Proposed next steps
- First experiment (proposed 12 weeks): use held-out normal captures from ArmaturaSec archives for one Modbus TCP site and one BACnet/IP site (BACnet capture availability to be confirmed; Kiss’s documented testbed is Modbus/DNP3, so do not assume it supplies BACnet). Train a per-site baseline on an early normal window and hold out later normal windows; compare against a fixed-threshold rule and a static Gaussian baseline. Kiss proposes feature and calibration design and analysis; ArmaturaSec proposes archive access, bench or mirrored segment, firmware integration, and one part-time engineer. Inject controlled anomalies one factor at a time. Proposed go/no-go targets: ≤1 false alarm per site per day on held-out normal; ≥80% recall on injected anomalies; no packet loss and p99 forwarding-latency increase within an agreed bound; an ArmaturaSec-nominated plant-facing reviewer can explain each alert card unaided, with pilot plant-manager testing only if consenting clients are secured; BACnet no-go if no BACnet normal sample is available.
- If the first experiment passes, run a calibration and drift study on ArmaturaSec multi-site normal archives: compare static versus incremental updates and measure seasonal or process-change false alarms, testing whether Kiss’s testbed-calibrated recalibration transfers to company traffic.
- Port the selected detector to the agreed ProtoSense or NetGuard target under NDA and measure CPU, memory, and forwarding latency on the hardware bench; if the planned security-processor variant is unavailable, use the existing appliance as baseline.
- Conditional on ArmaturaSec securing two consenting pilot clients, co-design an alert card with their plant managers and measure whether they can judge an alert actionable unaided; otherwise use ArmaturaSec engineer review and defer the plant-manager test.

## Open questions
- Does Krisztina Kiss have availability and supervisory capacity for a joint project in the coming academic year, and can her group’s testbed data-sharing agreement be applied to ArmaturaSec?
- Which ArmaturaSec traffic archives and BACnet/IP captures can be shared under NDA, for which sites and time periods, and do they include any known incidents or operator annotations?
- What target hardware and resource budget should the first prototype meet: existing ProtoSense or NetGuard appliances or the planned late-2025 security-processor variant?
- What false-positive rate, alert volume, and explanation format would be acceptable to ArmaturaSec’s clients and plant managers, and can two consenting pilot plant managers be secured for explanation testing?
- What approvals and licensing terms are needed before controlled anomaly injection on a bench or mirrored segment and joint code integration can begin?

inferences: Transfer is untested: the researcher's evidence comes from news, legal, encyclopedia-style and web corpora, while LinguaBot queries include mid-word script typos and bank support vocabulary.
Manual dictionary upkeep is likely a risk: the researcher's pilot paper notes modules need updating for new terminology, and the company's synonym-list experience points the same way.

proposedActions: First experiment (months 1–2): test on the 12,000-query miss sample, with the 85,000 labelled pairs as held-out validation. Baseline: current Elasticsearch pipeline with the Croatian stemmer. Change one suspected factor at a time. Measure the company's 'no useful result' rate; add MRR@10 and P@5 if labels allow. Proposed go/no-go: proceed only if the best variant lowers no-useful-result by at least 5 absolute points versus baseline and stem-after-normalisation beats stem-only by a pre-registered margin; the below-5% target is tested in the six-month pilot, not assumed here. Proposed contributions: researcher supplies canonicalisation/stemming code and analysis; company supplies queries, labels, Elasticsearch config and linguist validation.

If it passes, build an Elasticsearch integration prototype for new product terminology using override rules plus an incremental update path, and test new-vocabulary queries without full re-indexing (months 3–4).
Run a held-out client pilot with linguist validation; proposed success criteria are below 5% no-useful-result rate and no P@5 degradation (months 5–6, subject to budget and availability).
Measure production latency and throughput against SLOs to be confirmed with the company, comparing deterministic-only and OOV neural fallback; do not claim hardware fit from model reduction alone.

content.markdown:
# Serbian Morphology and Script Canonicalisation for LinguaBot Search

## Verified facts
- The company reports that in a sample of 12,000 real support queries from one bank client, about 18% returned no useful result, with more than half of those misses traced to morphological mismatch or script confusion. [F1]
- The company's good outcome is getting that 18% miss rate below 5% and keeping it there with a manageable maintenance process. [F2]
- The company states a budget of around 8,000 EUR for tooling or data work and wants something testable within six months. [F3]
- The company requires an approach that tolerates script mixing automatically and can be updated when new vocabulary arrives without a full re-index. [F4]
- The company has around 85,000 labelled query-response pairs across clients, and two in-house linguists who can annotate or validate solutions. [F5]
- The researcher's group works on mixed Cyrillic–Latin Serbian retrieval, script normalisation, transliteration preprocessing and script-robust inverted indexes; his notes state capacity for one smaller industrial contract. [F6]
- The researcher's published method uses a phoneme-based canonical token form as the primary index identifier, reporting F1 0.81 in ad-hoc search, 14 points above the better of two baselines. [F7]
- The researcher's morphological paper reports stemming after normalisation gives consistently better results for all three combinations, evaluated on a CLEF 2012 subset with both scripts. [F8]

## Our inference
- Transfer is untested: the researcher's evidence comes from news, legal, encyclopedia-style and web corpora, while LinguaBot queries include mid-word script typos and bank support vocabulary.
- Manual dictionary upkeep is likely a risk: the researcher's pilot paper notes modules need updating for new terminology, and the company's synonym-list experience points the same way.
- The researcher's latency study reports a cost for neural normalisation and lower cost for a cascaded OOV fallback; production SLOs are unknown, so neural components should be optional.

## Proposed next steps
- First experiment (months 1–2): test on the 12,000-query miss sample, with the 85,000 labelled pairs as held-out validation. Baseline: current Elasticsearch pipeline with the Croatian stemmer. Run four variants on identical queries: script canonicalisation only, Serbian lemmatisation/stemming only, stem-after-normalisation, and deterministic normalisation with neural fallback only for out-of-vocabulary tokens. Change one suspected factor at a time. Measure the company's 'no useful result' rate; add MRR@10 and P@5 if labels allow. Proposed go/no-go: proceed only if the best variant lowers no-useful-result by at least 5 absolute points versus baseline and stem-after-normalisation beats stem-only by a pre-registered margin; the below-5% target is tested in the six-month pilot, not assumed here. Proposed contributions: researcher supplies canonicalisation/stemming code and analysis; company supplies queries, labels, Elasticsearch config and linguist validation.
- If it passes, build an Elasticsearch integration prototype for new product terminology using override rules plus an incremental update path, and test new-vocabulary queries without full re-indexing (months 3–4).
- Run a held-out client pilot with linguist validation; proposed success criteria are below 5% no-useful-result rate and no P@5 degradation (months 5–6, subject to budget and availability).
- Measure production latency and throughput against SLOs to be confirmed with the company, comparing deterministic-only and OOV neural fallback; do not claim hardware fit from model reduction alone.

## Open questions
- Your formal availability is unknown: can you confirm availability for a six-month joint project within the company's modest budget, given the note about one smaller industrial contract?
- Will LinguaBot provide the 85,000 labelled pairs and the 12,000-query sample, make the two in-house linguists available, and share mid-word script-mixing and stemmer-failure examples?
- What is the exact definition and per-client breakdown of 'no useful result', and how should the below-5% target be measured?
- Which Elasticsearch version and pipeline must the solution fit, what re-indexing or downtime is allowed for new vocabulary, and who owns override-rule updates after the project?
- What latency and throughput SLOs apply, and can a neural fallback be limited to out-of-vocabulary tokens?

proposedActions: Proposed first experiment: machine fatigue specimens from the two failed sections and from new production crossmember-to-stringer details in mild-steel hollow section, MIG/MAG welded and painted. Proposed success criterion: a measurable increase in cycles to crack initiation versus the current production detail, with the target agreed after baseline results.

content.markdown:
# Root cause and fatigue-life improvement of welded conveyor frames in cold stores

## Verified facts
- AutomVoj reports that it does not currently have the equipment or know-how to test at low temperatures under cyclic load. [F1]
- Cold-store conveyors typically operate at 2–6 °C, with suspected thermal cycling, condensation and loaded-belt vibration; the company tests frames under load at room temperature. [F2]
- AutomVoj has photos and measurements of cracked joints from site visits and still has two failed sections in storage. [F3]
- The frames are mild-steel hollow sections, painted for corrosion resistance, MIG/MAG welded, with cracking reported at main crossmember-to-stringer connections. [F4]
- Erić's group routinely uses servo-hydraulic fatigue machines, a climate chamber to −60 °C and Abaqus FE models; the chamber and machine are shared, so extended campaigns need advance coordination. [F5]
- AutomVoj states it has no dedicated R&D department and that technical development happens informally through project work. [F6]
- Erić is open to contract research on fatigue and fracture testing of welded steel components and to joint projects involving low-temperature or combined loading fatigue testing. [F7]
- In Erić's low-temperature study, cruciform fillet-welded S355J2+N specimens tested at −40 °C showed a 22% decrease in fatigue ductility coefficient relative to room temperature. [F8]

## Our inference
- Erić's combination of low-temperature fatigue testing, residual-stress measurement and FE analysis appears well matched to a root-cause study, but his published low-temperature data are on other steels and specimen types, so transfer to AutomVoj's mild-steel hollow-section detail at 2–6 °C must be tested rather than assumed.
- The 22% fatigue-ductility drop at −40 °C is a possible cold-service risk, not evidence about AutomVoj's frames at 2–6 °C; the first experiment should treat it as a hypothesis and check the transfer gap.
- Erić's residual-stress and post-weld heat-treatment work suggests welding procedure, filler or joint-design changes may lower weld-toe crack driving force, but the benefit for this production detail is unproven.

## Proposed next steps
- Proposed first experiment: machine fatigue specimens from the two failed sections and from new production crossmember-to-stringer details in mild-steel hollow section, MIG/MAG welded and painted. Run a common mechanical load spectrum at room-temperature dry baseline, 2–6 °C isothermal, and 2–6 °C with slow thermal cycling; add condensation as a separate condition if humidity control is available, changing one suspected factor at a time. Measure cycles to 5% stiffness drop, crack initiation at the weld toe and post-test crack location. Company contribution proposed: supply failed and new sections, weld procedure, filler, paint and any site vibration or load records; researcher contribution proposed: specimen design, shared climate-chamber/servo-hydraulic testing and fracture analysis. Go/no-go: proceed to mechanism study only if a cold or thermal condition shows a statistically significant life reduction versus the room-temperature baseline; if not, stop the thermal hypothesis and test vibration or condensation separately. Proposed duration: six-month feasibility phase.
- If the first experiment passes, compare welding procedure, filler material and joint-design variants, including post-weld heat treatment where applicable, under the worst condition identified. Proposed success criterion: a measurable increase in cycles to crack initiation versus the current production detail, with the target agreed after baseline results.
- Use FE and residual-stress measurements to rank the likely crack drivers and draft a revised joint detail or welding change. Proposed deliverable: a cause ranking and draft procedure change reviewed with AutomVoj's chief engineer.
- Proposed timeline as negotiation target: months 1–2 specimen preparation and shared chamber scheduling; months 3–6 first experiment; months 7–9 variant comparison if go; month 10 review and draft procedure change.

## Open questions
- Can Professor Erić confirm availability and a scheduling window for the shared climate chamber and servo-hydraulic machine, since current availability is unknown?
- Can AutomVoj name an engineering owner and allocate company time for the project despite having no dedicated R&D department?
- Can AutomVoj provide the two failed sections, photos and measurements, weld procedure, filler specification, paint system and any site vibration or load records?
- What exact crossmember-to-stringer geometry, hollow-section size, plate thickness and welding parameters should be replicated in test specimens?
- What cycle-life improvement or reduction in warranty replacements would AutomVoj accept as a go decision after the first experiment?
